overview:
Around 518 BCE, Darius I began levelling a vast terrace against the flank of the Kuh-e Rahmat, on the Marvdasht plain in what is now Fars province in southern Iran. The Persians called the place Parsa; the Greek name Persepolis, which stuck, means roughly "the Persian city." The terrace was part quarried rock and part built platform, and onto it went a century's worth of construction under Darius, his son Xerxes, and their successors: the Apadana or great audience hall, the monumental gateway Xerxes called the Gate of All Nations, the hundred-columned throne hall, treasuries, and a cluster of residential palaces. The materials were themselves an argument about empire — cedar hauled from Lebanon, gold from Lydia and Bactria, ivory from Nubia and India, stoneworkers and craftsmen drawn from across the subject lands. The stairway reliefs of the Apadana show delegations from every corner of the empire filing forward with gifts, each rendered in its own dress and bearing its own tribute, an image of orderly diversity under a single king that has no real precedent in the ancient world.

What Persepolis was actually for is still argued over. It was never the empire's only capital — Susa, Ecbatana and Babylon all served royal business, and the Achaemenid court moved between them — and the older idea that Persepolis existed mainly to stage the Nowruz new-year festival is a modern reconstruction rather than something the ancient sources state. Clearer is that the site was a working place as well as a symbolic one. Tens of thousands of clay tablets found in the fortification wall and the treasury, most of them written in Elamite and dating to roughly 509–493 BCE and after, record the mundane business of the region: rations of barley, wine and beer issued to travellers and work gangs, silver paid out as wages, fodder for animals, offerings to gods, travel authorizations for officials moving along the royal roads. They name women workers and their allotments, foreign labourers, and the administrators who sealed the documents. They are among the very few sources on the Persian empire written from inside it rather than by its Greek enemies.

In 330 BCE Alexander of Macedon took the site, stripped its treasuries, and burned the palaces. Greek and Roman writers could not agree on why: some framed it as calculated revenge for Xerxes' burning of Athens in 480, others as an act of drunken impulse at a banquet. The fire that consumed the cedar roofing also baked the clay archives hard enough to survive, which is why so much administrative detail exists at all. Persepolis was not resettled on any scale; the nearby town of Estakhr took over the region's life, and the terrace stood half-buried and visible for centuries, drawing travellers from at least the 1600s. Systematic excavation began only in 1931, when Ernst Herzfeld and then Erich Schmidt worked the site for the Oriental Institute of Chicago across eight seasons, employing crews of several hundred. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.
significance: Persepolis is the fullest surviving statement of how the Achaemenids wanted to be seen — not as conquerors flattening difference, but as a centre holding many peoples in place, each recognizable, each contributing. That visual language of empire, carved into stairways in the fifth century BCE, echoes through later Persian, Hellenistic and Roman monumental art. Its destruction became one of antiquity's set pieces, cited ever after as the moment the Persian empire visibly ended, and the ruins later served modern Iranian nationalism as a physical link to a pre-Islamic past — most conspicuously at the 1971 imperial celebrations staged in tents at the foot of the terrace. And the clay tablets accidentally preserved by Alexander's fire remain the single richest body of evidence for how the largest empire the world had yet seen actually fed, paid and moved its people.
coverage: The dataset holds no events at all beneath this story, so nothing here is drawn from it — the account comes from reference works and the excavation record. Beyond that, the deeper gap is in the ancient record itself: the Achaemenids left royal inscriptions and reliefs that state ideology rather than narrate events, so almost every account of Persepolis in action, including its destruction, reaches us through Greek and Roman writers hostile to Persia and writing generations later. Even the site's basic purpose, its relationship to the other royal capitals, and the true scale of its settled population remain contested; the tens of thousands of administrative tablets are still only partly published and translated.
